The second failure is the fixed order. Circumstances genuinely reorder the priorities. In cold-water immersion the shelter interval collapses below the air interval — a person in 5 °C water may be incapacitated by cold shock and swim failure within minutes, so thermal protection is the immediate problem, not a later one. In desert heat with heavy exertion, water and shelter merge into a single problem and can outrank everything. For a diabetic on insulin, or a person with a metabolic disorder, or a small child with limited glycogen stores, food can become an hours-scale emergency rather than a weeks-scale one. Someone bleeding heavily has a seconds-to-minutes problem that precedes all four.

The third failure is scope. The rule says nothing about injury, infection, medication dependence, envenomation, altitude illness, decompression illness, or the many ordinary medical emergencies that continue to occur in the wilderness at roughly the rates they occur anywhere else. A person having a heart attack in a survival situation is having a heart attack. The rule is a triage device for environmental deprivation, not a system of medicine.

The fourth failure is that it says nothing about rescue. Survival narratives that end well almost always involve being found, and being found depends on things the rule never mentions: telling somebody your plan before you leave, carrying a personal locator beacon or satellite messenger, staying put, making yourself visually and thermally large, using contrast against the background, and having any signalling device at all. A signal mirror weighs 20 grams and has been effective at distances beyond 15 kilometres in good conditions. A whistle carries far further than a voice and costs no energy.

The fifth and subtlest failure is that the rule flatters preparation as a substitute for judgement. Somebody who has memorised it may believe they are prepared. The reality is that outcomes in the field correlate with fitness, navigation competence, appropriate clothing, having told someone where you were going, turning back early, and being willing to look foolish. The rule helps once things have already gone wrong; it does not reduce the chance that they will.

sections.heading: When It Goes Wrong: Deterioration, Rescue and Aftermath
sections.body:
The most useful thing to hold onto when a situation deteriorates is that survival outcomes are usually decided by a series of small, boring maintenance actions rather than by a single dramatic one. When conditions worsen, the discipline is to shrink your goals rather than abandon them. Cannot build a proper shelter? Get behind a rock and get insulation under you. Cannot purify water? Drink from the cleanest available source and accept the gastrointestinal risk, because dehydration will hurt you within a day and Giardia will not for at least a week. Cannot light a fire? Focus everything on insulation and shared body heat. Trading a certainty against a probability is almost always correct in this direction.

Recognising your own deterioration is genuinely difficult, because the failures are cognitive. Hypothermia, dehydration and exhaustion all impair insight before they impair function noticeably, and the standard field countermeasure is to externalise judgement — set decision rules in advance and follow them mechanically. Decide now, while warm, that you will stop and shelter at a fixed time regardless of how far you have got. Decide now that if you have not urinated in eight hours you will stop and drink. Written rules and companions who are authorised to enforce them outperform in-the-moment judgement by a wide margin.

If there is a group, the group's dynamics matter as much as its equipment. Assign roles, because unassigned tasks go undone. Pool resources rather than defending individual kit. Watch the quietest member, because withdrawal is the first sign of hypothermia and of despair. Share warmth deliberately; two people in one shelter with combined insulation are dramatically better off than two people separately.

If rescue arrives, be a good patient. Severely cold, dehydrated or starved people are physiologically fragile in ways that are invisible: gentle handling, horizontal transport, slow rewarming and slow refeeding are not fussiness but are the difference between recovery and a fatal arrhythmia. Do not walk out under your own power if you have been severely hypothermic and a stretcher is available. Do not eat a large meal after a long fast. Do not drink several litres of water quickly after prolonged deprivation, because rapid dilution can cause hyponatraemia, which kills by cerebral oedema; small frequent volumes with some salt are safer.

Afterwards, expect a psychological tail. Survivors of prolonged emergencies commonly report intrusive memories, sleep disturbance, guilt about decisions made and about companions who did not make it, and a period of emotional flatness. These are ordinary responses and generally resolve; where they do not, they respond well to treatment. The last piece of the Rule of Threes, unspoken in every version of it, is that surviving the event and recovering from it are two separate tasks, and the second one is not finished on the day you are found.

guides.safetyNote: The numbers in the Rule of Threes are memory pegs, not survival guarantees. Real limits vary enormously with temperature, exertion, body size, wetness, illness and age. People have died of hypothermia in under an hour in cold water and of dehydration in under a day in desert heat. Treat every figure here as an order-of-magnitude reminder of what to fix first, never as permission to delay. If a casualty is unconscious and not breathing normally, start chest compressions immediately and get emergency help; nothing else in this guide outranks that.

guides.title: Ordering Survival Priorities Correctly
guides.summary: How to work out what to do first when things go wrong: the physiology behind the survival priority hierarchy, where the familiar Rule of Threes misleads, and how to reorder priorities correctly for the environment and circumstances you are actually in.
guides.safetyNote: Priority frameworks are decision aids, not substitutes for training. Life-threatening bleeding, airway obstruction and anaphylaxis outrank every item in any survival hierarchy and need hands-on first-aid competence learned in advance. If a means of calling for help exists, use it early rather than late; self-rescue attempts that fail usually make the situation worse.

sections.heading: Sequence Beats Skill
sections.body: Most people who die in survival situations are not killed by a lack of skills. They are killed by doing the right things in the wrong order. This is the single most important idea in the entire subject, and it is consistently underemphasised because sequencing is dull to teach and skills are exciting. A person who can build a beautiful friction fire but spends the first two hours of a cold wet evening gathering firewood while soaked to the skin has made a fatal error, and no amount of technique will retrieve it. A person with almost no skills who gets out of the wind, gets dry, and stays put has done the important part. The reason ordering dominates is that survival situations are governed by competing clocks running at wildly different speeds. Oxygen deprivation kills in minutes. Uncontrolled bleeding kills in minutes. Loss of core temperature kills in hours. Dehydration kills in days. Starvation kills in weeks. Because these timescales differ by factors of thousands, an error in ordering is not a small inefficiency; it is spending the resource you have least of on the problem that mattered least. Every hour is finite, and so is every calorie, every litre of body water, and every unit of daylight, warmth and clear thinking. Once spent on the wrong problem they are not recoverable. There is a second, subtler reason. Effort itself is expensive. Building a shelter, gathering wood, or walking out are not free actions that can be attempted speculatively. A substantial debris shelter can cost well over a thousand kilocalories and a litre or more of sweat, which in a hot dry environment can convert a survivable situation into a lethal one. Doing something is not automatically better than doing nothing. Choosing correctly between them is the whole discipline. The same logic applies far beyond wilderness emergencies. A house fire, a road accident, a medical crisis at home, a power failure in deep winter and a boat taking water are all situations in which the outcome turns on what is attended to in the first few minutes, and in which the natural human impulse is to attend to whatever is loudest rather than whatever is fastest. A third reason is that the decisions interact. Deciding to walk out changes your water requirement, your heat production, your injury risk and, critically, your findability, because search efforts concentrate near the point you were last known to be. Deciding to light a fire changes your signalling, your morale and your thermal balance at once. These are not independent choices to be optimised separately. What follows sets out the standard priority frameworks, explains the physiology that generates them, and then does the more useful and less commonly attempted job of explaining where those frameworks are wrong, how the correct order changes with environment and circumstance, and how to reorder deliberately rather than by instinct. The aim is not a list to memorise but the ability to derive the right order for the situation you are actually in.

sections.heading: The Rule of Threes: What It Says and Why It Works
sections.body: The most widely taught ordering device is the Rule of Threes. In its usual form it states that a person can survive roughly three minutes without air, three hours without shelter in harsh conditions, three days without water, and three weeks without food. Some versions prefix three seconds without thinking, or append three months without companionship. Its origin is genuinely obscure. It appears in survival instruction through the second half of the twentieth century without a clear original author, and it has the character of an oral teaching device refined by repetition rather than a finding derived from research. That does not make it wrong. It makes it a mnemonic whose authority comes from correspondence with physiology rather than from a citation. What it gets right is the essential point, which is the ordering and the orders of magnitude. Each step changes the timescale by roughly a factor of twenty to fifty, and that spacing is real. Air, warmth, water and food genuinely are the four requirements, and they genuinely do have that priority in most circumstances. Anyone who internalises nothing else has still acquired the single most valuable structural insight available, namely that food is almost never the problem and that people who spend their first day looking for berries have inverted the hierarchy completely. The rule also encodes a useful psychological correction. Hunger is a loud, insistent, well-known sensation and appears early. Dehydration announces itself somewhat later and less clearly. Hypothermia is famously insidious and impairs the judgement that would recognise it. The subjective urgency of these problems is almost exactly inverse to their real urgency, and the rule exists partly to overrule your own sensations. Anyone who has been cold, wet and hungry can attest that the hunger is what occupies the mind, and the hypothermia is what will kill them. It is worth noticing what the rule quietly asserts by omission. It does not mention finding your way, building a fire, catching animals, purifying water or any of the activities that dominate popular survival entertainment. Those are means, not ends, and several of them serve more than one end at once, which is precisely why they are so easily mistaken for priorities in their own right. Fire is not a survival priority; warmth is, and fire happens to be one way of achieving it, alongside insulation, shelter and movement, each of which may be cheaper in a given situation. Understood properly, the three numbers are not predictions but categories. Three minutes means immediately, drop everything. Three hours means today, this is your afternoon's work. Three days means soon, plan for it now and act within the day. Three weeks means later, and probably means never, because virtually every survival incident in the modern world resolves one way or another long before starvation becomes relevant. Read that way the rule is excellent. Read as a set of literal survival times it is misleading in ways that have contributed to deaths, and the specific ways it fails are worth understanding as precisely as the rule itself.

sections.heading: Where the Rule of Threes Misleads
sections.body: The Rule of Threes is a good mnemonic and a poor model, and the gap between the two matters. Four of its failures are serious enough to correct explicitly. First, the numbers are not survival times, they are rough medians under unstated conditions, and the real variance is enormous. Three days without water is approximately right for a resting adult in temperate shade and grossly optimistic in desert heat, where a person working in 40 degree Celsius conditions can lose 1 to 1.5 litres of sweat per hour and be dead well inside 24 hours. It is equally pessimistic in a cold, humid environment where water losses are low. Three weeks without food underestimates most healthy adults substantially; medically supervised total fasts and the historical record of hunger strikes suggest that death typically occurs somewhere between 45 and 70 days in a person of normal build with adequate water, and the Irish hunger strike of 1981, in which Bobby Sands died on day 66, is a documented reference point. Three hours without shelter is meaningless without specifying conditions: in cold water it can be under one hour, and on a mild dry night it may be indefinite. Second, the rule omits the two fastest killers of all. Catastrophic haemorrhage from a major artery can empty a person in around three minutes, faster than airway obstruction in many cases, and it is far more common in wilderness incidents than asphyxiation. Anaphylaxis operates on a similar clock. Neither appears in the rule, yet both outrank everything in it. Third, the rule is silent on rescue, which in the modern world is usually the actual solution. Most lost person incidents in countries with organised search and rescue are resolved within 24 hours, which means that being found is normally a far more effective survival strategy than being self-sufficient. A framework that lists shelter, water and food but not signalling gives no weight to the thing most likely to end the emergency. Fourth, the rule presents a fixed order when the correct order is context-dependent. In a hot desert, water and shade are effectively the same problem and both outrank almost everything. In cold water, thermal protection outranks everything including signalling, because you will be unconscious before a search begins. On a mountain in a storm, shelter is so dominant that water can wait a full day. Treating the sequence as fixed produces confident, well-executed, wrong decisions. The practical repair is straightforward. Keep the rule as a first approximation, then explicitly ask which clock is running fastest here, right now, for me, and act on that answer rather than on the recited order. Adding two items covers most of the gap: put stop the bleeding and secure the airway above everything, and insert make yourself findable immediately after the thermal problem is under control. A revised working order of bleeding and airway, then warmth, then signalling, then water, then food is a better default than the original for almost every incident that occurs in a country with functioning emergency services.

sections.heading: Why the Clocks Run at Those Speeds: Oxygen and the Brain
sections.body: The priority order is not arbitrary. It falls directly out of how the body stores and uses each resource, and understanding the mechanism lets you adapt the order intelligently instead of reciting it. Oxygen sits first because the body stores almost none of it. The lungs, blood and tissues together hold perhaps a litre and a half of usable oxygen, against a resting consumption of roughly 250 millilitres per minute, so the entire reserve is a few minutes at best and far less under exertion. The brain is the constraint. It represents about 2 per cent of body mass but consumes around 20 per cent of resting oxygen, and it has essentially no anaerobic capacity. If cerebral circulation stops completely, consciousness is lost in about 10 to 15 seconds, and irreversible neuronal damage begins after roughly 4 to 6 minutes at normal body temperature. This is the origin of the three-minute figure and of the urgency in every airway and drowning protocol. An important refinement is that cooling extends this window substantially, because metabolic rate falls roughly 6 to 7 per cent for every degree Celsius drop in core temperature. This is why cold-water drowning victims, particularly children, have been resuscitated after submersion times of 30 minutes or more, and it is the basis of the emergency medicine maxim that no one is dead until they are warm and dead. It is also why the same physiology that makes cold dangerous can, in one specific circumstance, be protective. Airway obstruction deserves separate mention because it is the mechanism most amenable to immediate action and the one most often present in wilderness deaths that get recorded as something else. An unconscious person lying on their back can obstruct their own airway with the tongue within seconds, which is why the recovery position is a genuinely life-saving intervention requiring no equipment and about three seconds of decision. Carbon monoxide and hypoxic atmospheres are the quiet variants of the same clock, and they matter because they defeat the warning system. Carbon monoxide binds haemoglobin with an affinity roughly 200 to 250 times that of oxygen, so a small concentration disables a large fraction of the blood's carrying capacity while producing only headache and confusion. Every year people die from stoves, heaters and fires burning inside tents, snow shelters and vehicles, precisely because the action that solved the cold problem created an invisible oxygen problem which outranks it. Similarly, a snow cave or a sealed shelter can accumulate carbon dioxide. The general principle is that any intervention on a slower clock must not create a problem on a faster one, and this is the commonest way that competent survival actions kill people.

sections.heading: The Thermal Clock: Why Temperature Usually Wins
sections.body: Temperature is the priority that most often decides real outcomes, and it is worth understanding as a balance rather than as a sensation. The body is a heat engine producing roughly 100 watts at rest, rising to 300 or 400 watts during hard work and up to a kilowatt briefly in athletes. Core temperature holds near 37 degrees Celsius only while production matches loss. If loss exceeds production, core temperature falls; if production exceeds the body's ability to shed heat, it rises. Survival in either direction is a matter of manipulating the terms. Heat leaves the body by four routes and knowing their relative sizes tells you where to intervene. Conduction is direct contact, and it is the one people neglect: water conducts heat roughly 25 times faster than still air, and the cold ground beneath a person lying down can extract heat faster than any wind. This is why insulation underneath you matters more than insulation over you, and why a sleeping mat is worth more than an extra blanket. Convection is moving air or water carrying heat away, and it scales sharply with wind speed; this is the mechanism behind wind chill. Radiation is infrared emission toward cold surfaces including a clear night sky, and it is the reason a clear night is far colder than an overcast one at the same air temperature. Evaporation is the loss from sweat and from breath, which is the dominant cooling route in heat and an unwanted loss in cold. Two facts drive most cold casualties. First, wet clothing loses the great majority of its insulating value, because the trapped air that does the insulating is displaced by water, and down loses essentially all of it. Getting dry is therefore usually a larger intervention than getting warm, and it is almost always cheaper. Second, hypothermia degrades exactly the faculty needed to fix it. Mild hypothermia between 32 and 35 degrees Celsius brings shivering, clumsiness and impaired judgement; between 28 and 32 shivering stops, confusion deepens, and the characteristic paradoxical undressing sometimes appears; below 28 degrees consciousness and then cardiac rhythm fail. The victim's decision-making is compromised well before the situation is obviously serious, which is why cold demands pre-emptive action rather than reactive. Cold water compresses the whole sequence. Gordon Giesbrecht's widely taught 1-10-1 framing captures it: roughly one minute to bring the cold shock gasping reflex under control, about ten minutes of useful movement before hands and arms stop working, and around one hour before unconsciousness from hypothermia. The first minute kills more people than the hour, because the gasp reflex causes inhalation of water. Heat illness runs the same balance in reverse, and heatstroke, defined by a core temperature above about 40 degrees with neurological signs, is a genuine emergency in which minutes of cooling matter. In hot environments, shade and cessation of work are the interventions, and they are inseparable from the water problem because sweat is the only effective cooling route available.

sections.heading: The Water Clock: Losses, Timelines and the Rationing Error
sections.body: Water sits third in the standard hierarchy but frequently moves higher, and understanding why requires looking at losses rather than at some fixed daily requirement. A resting adult in a temperate climate loses roughly 2 to 3 litres a day through urine, breath, insensible skin loss and faeces. That is the baseline. Everything else is added on top. Working hard in heat, sweat rates of 1 to 1.5 litres per hour are routine and rates above 2 litres per hour are recorded, so a day of exertion in a desert can cost more than ten litres. Breathing very cold dry air also costs significant water, which is why dehydration is a real and under-recognised problem in winter mountaineering where nobody feels thirsty. The consequences track the deficit closely. A loss of about 2 per cent of body mass, which is around 1.5 litres in a 75 kilogram adult, already produces measurable declines in endurance, concentration and decision quality. Around 5 per cent brings headache, marked fatigue, and irritability. Around 10 per cent produces serious physiological compromise, and losses in the region of 15 to 20 per cent are generally fatal. The three-day figure is a reasonable central estimate for a resting adult in temperate shade; it can stretch beyond a week in cool humid conditions and collapse to under 24 hours in desert heat with exertion. This spread is why water can outrank shelter in one environment and sit well below it in another. The most important practical correction concerns rationing. The instinct on discovering a limited water supply is to ration it, drinking small sips to make it last. This is physiologically wrong. Water held in a bottle does nothing; water in your tissues maintains blood volume, cognition and the ability to sweat. The long-standing desert maxim is to ration sweat, not water: drink what you need and reduce your losses instead, by resting in shade during the heat of the day, moving at night, staying clothed to reduce evaporative and radiative load, and not talking more than necessary. Deaths have occurred in people found with water still in their containers. Two further points matter for ordering. Thirst is an unreliable indicator and lags the actual deficit, particularly in the cold and in older people, so drinking should be scheduled rather than felt. And the question of whether to drink water of doubtful quality is usually decided in favour of drinking: waterborne illness typically takes days to develop and is often survivable, whereas dehydration is acting now. Treating water when you can is clearly better, but withholding available water from a dehydrating person because it cannot be purified inverts the clocks. The exception is water that is chemically contaminated rather than biologically, such as run-off near industry, mine drainage or salt water, none of which becomes safe with time and salt water actively accelerates dehydration by demanding more water to excrete than it provides.

sections.heading: The Food Clock: Why Eating Comes Last
sections.body: Food is the priority people most consistently overrate, and the overestimate is worth dismantling carefully because the effort spent on it is drawn directly from the budget available for problems that will actually kill you. The body carries substantial energy reserves. Liver and muscle glycogen together amount to roughly 1,500 to 2,000 kilocalories and are largely depleted within about 24 hours of fasting. What follows is a well characterised metabolic transition. The liver produces glucose from amino acids and from the glycerol backbone of fats, a process called gluconeogenesis, and within two to three days ketone bodies rise sufficiently for the brain to derive a large fraction of its energy from them rather than from glucose. This adaptation is the reason humans tolerate fasting so well: it spares muscle protein by switching the largest glucose consumer onto fat. Body fat is a very large store. A lean adult carrying 12 kilograms of fat holds on the order of 100,000 kilocalories, which at a reduced resting expenditure is many weeks of fuel. The empirical record supports this. Healthy adults with access to water have survived total fasts of 45 to 70 days, and the 1981 Irish hunger strikes provide documented timelines, with Bobby Sands dying on the sixty-sixth day. The extreme outlier is the case of Angus Barbieri, a severely obese man who fasted under medical supervision with vitamin and electrolyte supplementation for 382 days in the mid-1960s and survived, which demonstrates the size of the fat reserve while illustrating nothing safe or replicable. What matters for ordering is that essentially no survival incident in the modern world lasts long enough for starvation to be the cause of death. People are found, walk out, or die of cold, injury or dehydration long before. Spending the first day of an incident foraging is therefore not merely a low-value activity, it is a negative one: it costs calories, costs water through sweat, costs daylight, moves you away from the point you were last seen, and carries a real risk of poisoning from misidentified plants. Two qualifications keep this honest. First, food does matter for morale and for warmth, since digestion raises heat production modestly and eating is psychologically stabilising, so easily obtained calories are worth taking. Second, hypoglycaemia in a diabetic person, and energy depletion in a child, in a very lean person or in someone already exhausted, can become urgent on a scale of hours rather than weeks. The general rule holds for healthy adults and should not be applied blindly to everyone. The correct posture toward food, then, is opportunism rather than pursuit. Eat what is already in your pack. Take calories that cost almost nothing to acquire, such as fruit within arm's reach of where you are already sitting. Do not organise your day around obtaining them, do not travel for them, and do not eat anything you cannot identify with certainty, since a gastrointestinal illness that costs you fluid is a straightforward loss on a clock that is running much faster than hunger.

sections.heading: The Priority Before All Priorities: Stop Making It Worse
sections.body: Before any of the physiological clocks, there is a step that costs nothing, takes minutes, and has probably saved more lives than every other survival skill combined. It is to stop moving and think. The reason it needs stating is that human behaviour under sudden threat is poor by default. Field observations by researchers including the psychologist John Leach have repeatedly found a similar pattern in disasters: a minority, often put at around 10 to 15 per cent, act purposefully; the large majority, commonly estimated near 70 to 80 per cent, become stunned, passive and bewildered, doing very little; and a small remainder behave counterproductively, with panic, freezing or dangerous impulsivity. These proportions are approximate and derived from observation rather than controlled experiment, so they should be treated as a robust qualitative finding rather than precise statistics. The qualitative finding is what matters: doing nothing useful is the normal response, not the exceptional one, and this is not a failure of character. The compounding danger is that the first instinct in a lost or stranded situation is usually to move, quickly, in the direction that feels right. This is close to the worst available action. It burns calories and water, increases injury risk on unfamiliar ground, generally happens while judgement is already degraded, and above all it moves you away from the point where you were last known to be, which is where any search will start and concentrate. A great many fatal wilderness cases consist of someone walking energetically in the wrong direction for a day. The standard countermeasure is the mnemonic STOP: Stop, Think, Observe, Plan. Its value lies in inserting a deliberate pause between the shock and the first action, so that the first action is chosen rather than reflexive. Sitting down is a surprisingly effective physical component, because it makes leaving harder and gives the acute stress response a few minutes to subside enough for reasoning to return. Eating a small amount and drinking, if you have them, helps for the same reason. Attitude has a genuine effect, though the popular treatment of it is overstated. What the evidence supports is fairly specific: people who believe their actions matter to the outcome persist longer, ration effort better, and are more likely to keep signalling and keep insulating on day three. People who conclude that nothing they do will change anything stop performing the small maintenance tasks that keep them alive. Setting concrete, small, achievable goals is the practical technique, because completing them supplies evidence against helplessness. Claims that a positive mental attitude alone determines survival, however, go beyond what anyone can demonstrate, and treating morale as a substitute for insulation is its own kind of error.

sections.heading: Medical Emergencies Override Everything
sections.body: The survival hierarchy assumes an uninjured person, and that assumption fails in a large fraction of real incidents, which begin with a fall, a vehicle accident, a burn or an animal encounter. Where a life-threatening injury is present, it outranks the entire framework, and the ordering within medical care is itself a priority system worth knowing. The most useful modern sequence is the MARCH order, developed in military medicine and now widespread in civilian wilderness and tactical care. Massive haemorrhage comes first, then Airway, then Respiration, then Circulation, then Hypothermia and Head injury. This is a deliberate revision of the older ABC ordering, and the change was driven by data: catastrophic external bleeding kills faster than almost anything else, and it is frequently correctable with simple equipment. A severed femoral artery can drain enough blood to cause death in roughly three minutes, comparable to airway obstruction, which is why the sequence was reordered to put bleeding first. For bleeding, direct firm pressure is the first intervention and works in most cases. Where it does not, a tourniquet placed high on the limb, tightened until the bleeding stops, and left in place is the correct action; the old fear that a tourniquet inevitably costs the limb has been substantially revised by combat experience showing good outcomes with application times of two hours and beyond. Note the time. Airway management in the field is mostly positioning. An unconscious breathing casualty belongs in the recovery position, on their side, letting gravity keep the tongue and any fluid clear. It needs no equipment at all. Hypothermia's presence at the end of MARCH is not an afterthought but a recognition that injured people lose heat very fast. Blood loss impairs thermoregulation, shock reduces perfusion, and a casualty lying still on cold ground cools far faster than an active person. The lethal triad of hypothermia, acidosis and impaired clotting is well documented in trauma care, and cooling directly worsens bleeding by degrading the clotting cascade. Insulating a casualty from the ground is therefore a trauma intervention, not merely comfort. Two other conditions belong in this fastest tier. Anaphylaxis can obstruct the airway within minutes and is treated with intramuscular adrenaline, which is why anyone with a known severe allergy should carry two auto-injectors. And tension pneumothorax after chest trauma can kill in minutes. Realistically, the decisive variable in all of this is whether the skills and equipment were acquired before the incident. A tourniquet cannot be improvised well under pressure by someone who has never handled one, and the improvised versions made from belts and sticks are markedly less effective than a purpose-made windlass device costing very little and weighing under 100 grams. Once the immediate medical threats are controlled, the ordinary hierarchy resumes, but with the injured person's altered clocks. An injured casualty loses heat faster, cannot maintain their own shelter, may be unable to drink unaided, and is far less able to move. This usually settles the stay-or-go question decisively in favour of staying and signalling, which is worth recognising early rather than after a failed attempt to carry someone.

sections.heading: Signalling and Rescue: The Priority the Rule Forgets
sections.body: In almost every survival incident in a country with organised emergency services, the situation ends because somebody finds you or because you reach help, not because you achieved self-sufficiency. This makes findability a first-order priority that deserves to sit immediately after the immediate physiological threats, and its omission from the Rule of Threes is that rule's largest practical defect. The statistics support the emphasis. Analysis of large search-and-rescue datasets, notably the work behind the International Search and Rescue Incident Database compiled by Robert Koester, shows that a large majority of lost-person incidents resolve within 24 hours, and that subjects are typically found surprisingly close to the point last seen, often within a few kilometres, and frequently much less in difficult terrain. Survival probability declines sharply with elapsed time, which means anything that shortens the search is worth a great deal. Three principles follow. The first is to make the search easier rather than the survival longer. Staying put, in one place, near your last known position, is usually the highest-value decision available, and it is the opposite of what instinct suggests. If you must move, leave clear markers of direction and time. The second is that electronic signalling dominates everything else where it exists. A personal locator beacon or satellite messenger transmitting on the 406 megahertz Cospas-Sarsat system delivers your position to a rescue coordination centre within minutes and typically to within about 100 metres, converting a search into a collection. A mobile phone, even without a usable signal for calls, may still connect to emergency services, may register on a network for later location analysis, and holds a bright light. Conserve battery aggressively by switching to flight mode between attempts and keeping the device warm, since cold dramatically reduces lithium battery capacity. The third is that passive signals work while you sleep and active ones do not. Contrast, geometry and movement are what aircraft and searchers detect: bright fabric spread flat in an open area, large geometric shapes laid out on the ground, smoke by day and fire by night, and reflective surfaces. A signal mirror is disproportionately effective, visible over many kilometres in sunlight for essentially no weight or power. Three of anything is the internationally recognised distress convention, whether whistle blasts, fires, or flashes; six blasts per minute is the standard mountain distress signal in Europe. A whistle carries far further than a voice and costs almost no energy, which is why it belongs on every jacket. The largest single contribution to your own rescue, however, is made before you leave. Telling a specific person where you are going, which route, and when you will be back converts an open-ended search of unlimited terrain into a bounded one along a known line, and it determines when anyone starts looking at all. People have died within a few hundred metres of a road because nobody knew to look for them. A trip plan left with someone reliable costs two minutes and is worth more than most of the equipment in a pack.

sections.heading: Reordering by Environment: Six Worked Cases
sections.body: The correct sequence is a function of environment, and the differences are large enough that a single memorised order will be badly wrong somewhere. Working through the major environments shows how the reasoning transfers. In cold water the order collapses almost entirely into thermal protection and flotation. Cold shock in the first minute causes involuntary gasping that drowns people before hypothermia is remotely relevant, so the first action is to control breathing and stay afloat. Then get as much of the body out of the water as possible, onto anything, since air at the same temperature extracts heat far more slowly. Do not swim for distant shore, because swimming increases heat loss substantially and most people badly overestimate their range in cold water. Adopt the heat escape lessening posture, knees drawn up and arms held in, or huddle with others. Water and food are irrelevant on this timescale. In hot desert the water and thermal problems merge, and shade during the heat of the day is the single highest-value action because it directly reduces water loss. Ground surface temperatures can exceed 60 to 70 degrees Celsius while air a metre up is far cooler, so getting off the ground matters. Stay clothed, since bare skin loses water faster and gains radiant heat. Travel at night if travel is necessary. Do not ration water. In cold mountains shelter and insulation dominate everything, and the priority within shelter is getting dry and getting off the ground. Water needs attention on day one despite the absence of thirst, because cold dry air and exertion produce large unnoticed losses and dehydration accelerates hypothermia. In humid jungle the ordering shifts again. Shelter is needed for rain rather than cold, water is usually abundant but almost always contaminated, and the dominant slow threats are infection from minor wounds, which fester rapidly in the heat and damp, and foot damage. Navigation is unusually hard and travel unusually costly, which strengthens the case for staying put. Keeping feet dry and treating small cuts immediately is a genuine priority rather than housekeeping. At sea, fresh water is the binding constraint and there is no source; drinking seawater accelerates death because excreting its salt load costs more water than it supplies. Sun protection and staying with the vessel or raft, which is far more visible than a swimmer, come next. In urban disaster the sequence changes character entirely. The threats are structural collapse, fire, contaminated water and loss of medication, and the resources are dense but disrupted. Here information and communication rise near the top, since knowing whether to shelter in place or evacuate determines everything, and medication continuity matters more than any wilderness skill.

sections.heading: The First Hour: A Working Procedure
sections.body: What follows is a sequence for the first hour after realising you are in trouble, written to be run in order. It resolves the competing clocks by handling the fastest first and deferring the slowest, and it deliberately puts thinking before acting, because the errors that kill people are almost all committed in the first fifteen minutes. It is written for a wilderness incident but the shape transfers: deal with what kills in minutes, then what kills in hours, then summon help, then settle in. Read it now, while nothing is wrong, because the whole point of a fixed sequence is that it can be followed by a frightened, cold person whose judgement has already begun to degrade.
steps: Stop where you are and sit down. Do not walk on, and do not walk back to look for the trail. The pause costs minutes; walking in the wrong direction costs the entire search effort and much of your energy budget.

Check for life-threatening injury in yourself and anyone with you, in the order massive bleeding, airway, breathing, circulation. Control catastrophic bleeding with direct pressure or a tourniquet before anything else, and put any unconscious breathing person on their side.

Call or signal for help now, not later, if any means exists. Activate a personal locator beacon or satellite messenger, or attempt an emergency call, before your battery is cold and flat and while daylight remains. Rescue is usually the fastest route out of the situation.

Assess your thermal situation honestly. Are you wet, is the wind on you, is the sun going down, what is the ground doing to you. If you are wet or cooling, fixing that outranks everything remaining, and getting dry and insulated from the ground is usually cheaper than building anything.
Inventory what you have, physically, laying it out. People routinely forget items in a pack under stress, and a bin liner, a foil blanket, a lighter or a whistle changes the plan entirely.

Decide explicitly whether to stay or go, and say the decision out loud with the reason. Stay is correct unless you are certain of the direction and distance, are uninjured, have the daylight and water for it, and nobody knows to look for you where you are.
Make yourself findable where you are. Move into open ground if any is nearby, spread bright material, prepare a fire, and set out anything that creates contrast or geometry from the air.
Sort water, treating it if you can and drinking what you have rather than hoarding it. Note any source you have already passed, since a known source behind you beats a hoped-for one ahead.
Improve shelter and insulation with the daylight that remains, working slowly enough not to sweat, since sweat soaks the insulation you are trying to build and costs water you cannot replace.
Leave food until last, and take only what costs nothing. Then rest, keep warm, keep signalling, and reassess at first light rather than acting on a night-time impulse.

sections.heading: Budgeting Effort: The Hidden Cost of Doing Something
sections.body: Every action in a survival situation is paid for in calories, water, heat and daylight, and the budget is finite. This is the consideration that separates people who make a bad situation survivable from people who exhaust themselves solving the wrong problem, and it is almost entirely absent from popular survival instruction, which tends to present activity as inherently virtuous. Consider the numbers. Hard physical work costs on the order of 400 to 600 kilocalories per hour and drives sweat rates of half a litre to two litres per hour depending on conditions. Building a substantial debris shelter is several hours of hard work, so it can plausibly cost 1,500 kilocalories and two or three litres of water. In a temperate forest with a stream nearby, that may be an excellent investment. In an arid environment with two litres of water remaining, it is close to suicidal, and the correct answer is to dig a shallow scrape in the shade of a rock and lie still. The same action is right in one place and lethal in another, and only the budget tells you which. Walking is the largest discretionary expenditure. A person carrying a light load on reasonable ground spends roughly 250 to 350 kilocalories per hour and rather more over rough terrain or uphill. A day's walking out can therefore cost two to three thousand kilocalories and several litres of water, which is why the stay-or-go decision is fundamentally an economic one rather than a matter of courage. The relevant questions are whether you know where you are going, whether you have the water for it, and whether anyone is coming. Sweating deserves specific attention as the most expensive habit in cold environments, because it costs water and it wets clothing, which then loses most of its insulating value, converting an energy expenditure into a thermal deficit. The technique used by polar travellers is to deliberately start cold, remove layers before beginning work, and work at a pace that never produces sweat. It feels wrong and it is correct. Sleep is an underrated part of the budget. Fatigue degrades decision-making severely, and most fatal sequences involve a bad decision made by an exhausted person. Resting is doing something. Similarly, heat conservation while resting, by insulating from the ground and reducing exposed surface area, saves calories that would otherwise be spent on shivering, which can raise metabolic rate several-fold. The general rule is to ask of any proposed action what it costs, what it buys, and whether anything cheaper buys the same thing. Very often something cheaper does. A pile of dry leaves stuffed inside clothing insulates nearly as well as a constructed shelter for a fraction of the effort. Sitting on a pack rather than the ground removes the largest conductive loss for no effort at all. Moving twenty metres to the lee of a boulder can be worth more than an hour of building. The habit of looking for the cheap version first is what makes a limited budget last, and it is the difference between arriving at the second day tired and arriving at it spent.

sections.heading: Planning Horizons: Hours, Days and Weeks Need Different Work
sections.body: A second dimension of ordering, distinct from urgency, is duration. The same problem deserves different solutions depending on how long the situation is expected to last, and matching the quality of a solution to the expected horizon prevents both under-building and the more common error of over-building. On a horizon of a few hours, which covers a night out in unplanned circumstances, everything should be improvised, cheap and reversible. The correct shelter is whatever gets you out of wind and off the ground in twenty minutes, not a structure. Water can generally wait. The correct posture is to conserve, keep signalling, and expect to walk out or be found in the morning. Most incidents live entirely at this horizon, which is why the elaborate skills people train for are so rarely the ones needed. On a horizon of a few days, which covers a genuine stranding with a search under way, the calculation changes. Water becomes a real problem and needs a source rather than a supply. Shelter is worth improving incrementally each day rather than building at once, since your energy budget is limited and the improvements compound. Signalling shifts from opportunistic to systematic, with prepared fires, laid-out ground markers and a routine. Hygiene begins to matter, since a gastrointestinal illness at this horizon is a serious water loss. Routine itself becomes valuable, giving structure to the day and protecting morale. On a horizon of weeks, which is rare outside genuinely remote regions and disasters, the priorities invert toward sustainability. Now a well-built shelter is worth the investment because it pays back over many nights. Now food genuinely enters the calculation, and calorie return per unit of effort becomes the governing criterion, which strongly favours fishing, trapping and gathering static resources over hunting, since active pursuit of animals is a famously poor energetic bargain. Now infection, dental problems, foot care and vitamin deficiency become real. The practical technique is to estimate the horizon explicitly and revise it. Ask who knows you are missing, when they will notice, how long a search will take to reach you, and what the weather will do. Then plan for roughly double that estimate and act accordingly. The characteristic error in both directions is instructive: people expecting rescue within hours build nothing and spend a dangerous night, while people who assume weeks exhaust themselves on day one constructing infrastructure they will abandon by lunchtime the next day when a helicopter arrives. Revising the estimate honestly, out loud, each morning is a better discipline than committing to either story. A useful hedge against getting the horizon wrong is to prefer solutions that improve incrementally. A shelter built in stages, starting with a windbreak and a ground layer and adding a roof, then thickening it, is never wasted at any horizon, whereas a shelter attempted all at once is either unfinished at nightfall or an overinvestment. The same applies to signalling, water and fire: do the cheap version now, and upgrade it only if tomorrow arrives and you are still there.

sections.heading: More Than One Person: Groups, Leadership and Sequencing
sections.body: Groups change the priority calculation substantially, mostly for the better, and the differences are worth anticipating because group dynamics under stress do not manage themselves. The advantages are real and large. Tasks can run in parallel, so one person can gather insulation while another prepares signals. Shared body heat is a genuine thermal resource, and huddling can be worth several degrees of effective temperature. A group can carry an injured person, can post a lookout, and can send a party for help while retaining someone at the last known position, which is often the ideal arrangement. Most importantly, more than one mind is available to notice errors, and stress-degraded judgement is partially correctable by another person asking why. The disadvantages are equally real. Groups move at the speed of their weakest member, and the water and food requirement scales with headcount while the shelter and fire requirement does not, which changes the arithmetic. Groups are prone to diffusion of responsibility, in which everyone assumes someone else is handling the signalling and nobody is. And they are prone to a collective drift in which nobody wants to be the one to say the situation is now serious, so the group continues acting as though the day is normal for hours after it has stopped being so. Two structural remedies address most of this. The first is explicit leadership, decided early and openly. It does not need to be the most experienced person, and it works better when the leader's job is defined as deciding and allocating rather than knowing everything. Rotating it is fine. What is not fine is leaving it implicit, because implicit leadership in a stressed group tends to fall to the loudest or the most confident, which correlates poorly with being right. The second is explicit task allocation by name: not someone should collect firewood but a named person collects firewood and reports back at a stated time. Naming defeats diffusion of responsibility, which is the same finding that underlies bystander effect research. Three further points matter. Decide the stay-or-go question as a group and commit, since splitting a group is usually a serious error and doubles the search problem. Attend to the weakest member first, because they will set the timetable regardless and hypothermia in one person rapidly becomes everyone's emergency. And talk. Verbalising the plan, the reasoning and the current priority keeps the group's model shared, catches errors, and does more for morale than encouragement does. Sending for help deserves its own rule. If a party leaves to fetch rescue, it should be at least two people where numbers allow, should carry written details of the location, the number of casualties and their condition, and should travel a route it is confident of rather than the shortest one. Those remaining stay exactly where the departing party left them, because a group that relocates after help has been summoned creates the worst possible outcome: rescuers arriving at a location the casualties have left.

sections.heading: How It Goes Wrong: Common Inversions and Mid-Incident Correction
sections.body: Knowing the correct order is not the same as following it, and the ways people invert it are consistent enough to be catalogued. Recognising your own inversion in progress is the most useful skill this whole subject can give you. The commonest inversion is food-first. It arises because hunger is the loudest signal, because foraging feels productive, and because popular survival media is preoccupied with it. Its cost is a day of daylight, a thousand calories, several litres of sweat, movement away from your last known position, and a real chance of poisoning, in exchange for solving the problem that would not have killed you for a month. The second is fire-first, in which a cold, wet person spends two hours gathering wood and attempting ignition while continuing to lose heat, when getting dry, getting out of the wind and getting off the ground would have solved the actual problem in twenty minutes with certainty. Fire is a means to warmth and often not the cheapest one. The third is walking-first, already described, and the most consequential. The fourth is gear-first, in which someone with equipment insists on using it in the way it was designed rather than solving the immediate problem with whatever is nearest. Underlying most inversions are three cognitive patterns. Plan continuation bias keeps people executing the original intention long after conditions have changed, and it is heavily documented in aviation accident analysis under the informal name get-there-itis. Sunk cost keeps people walking toward a destination because of the distance already covered. And normalcy bias delays the recognition that this is now an emergency, which is precisely the recognition that unlocks the correct priority order. Correcting mid-incident is possible and worth practising as a deliberate act. The trigger should be a scheduled one rather than a feeling: at every rest, and at least hourly, ask three questions aloud. What is the fastest clock running on me right now. What am I actually doing about it. And would I choose this action if I had just arrived here with no history. The last question is the strongest, because it strips out sunk cost and plan continuation in a single move. Accept the reversal gracefully when the answer changes. Turning back, abandoning a half-built shelter, or admitting that the route was wrong costs nothing but pride, and pride is the one resource you can afford to spend freely. The whole subject reduces to a short discipline that can be carried without equipment. Work out which clock is running fastest, spend your effort there and nowhere else, make yourself findable as early as possible, and re-ask the question every hour because the answer changes. Someone who does only that, with no skills, no gear and no experience, will outlive a far more capable person who is busy solving next week's problem with this afternoon's remaining energy. Ordering is not the introduction to the subject. It is the subject.

guides.title: The STOP Protocol for Sudden Emergencies
guides.summary: The four-step discipline behind the letters STOP - stop, think, observe, plan - what acute stress does to the body and mind that makes such a protocol necessary, how to run each step properly, and when stopping is exactly the wrong thing to do.

sections.heading: Four Letters Against the Worst Ten Minutes
sections.body:
Most emergencies are not lost at the moment they begin. They are lost in the ten or twenty minutes afterwards, during which a frightened person takes rapid, confident, badly reasoned action and converts a recoverable situation into an unrecoverable one. The lost walker who realises the trail is gone and immediately pushes faster downhill into thickening brush, adding two kilometres of error to an already wrong position. The driver who feels the car begin to slide and stamps the brake. The diver who cannot find the shot line and swims hard in a guessed direction, burning the gas that was the actual resource. The parent who runs into smoke. In each case the underlying problem was survivable, and the response made it fatal.

STOP is a memory device intended to interrupt precisely that sequence. The letters stand for Stop, Think, Observe, Plan. It is taught in wilderness and survival training, in scouting, in mountain rescue, in aviation and small-boat safety curricula, and in various renamed forms in nuclear power, in medicine and in the military. It is not clever. It does not tell you anything you did not already know. Its entire value lies in being short enough to survive the moment when your capacity to think has collapsed, and in occupying the seconds during which you would otherwise have done something irreversible.

That is worth stating plainly, because the protocol is often taught as though it were a decision-making method. It is not really. Real decision quality comes from knowledge, training and experience, none of which a four-letter word can supply. What STOP does is buy back the conditions under which whatever knowledge you already have can actually be used. A person in acute stress has most of their competence temporarily inaccessible; the skills are still there, but the systems that retrieve and apply them are degraded. STOP is a bridge across the first few minutes of that degradation. Anyone who has been through it will recognise the experience of realising, twenty minutes later and considerably calmer, that they knew the right answer the whole time.

The protocol also has a second, less obvious function: it converts an overwhelming, unbounded problem into a short sequence of small, bounded, answerable questions. Overwhelm is itself a major cause of paralysis. Asked what to do about being lost, a frightened person may genuinely be unable to answer. Asked what they can see, what they are carrying, how many hours of daylight remain and whether anyone knows where they went, the same person answers immediately and accurately. The questions are the mechanism. Getting from the first state to the second is the whole of the work, and it is why the protocol is ordered the way it is: a hard physical stop first, deliberate thought second, evidence-gathering third, and only then a plan.

sections.heading: What Acute Stress Does to the Body in the First Seconds
sections.body:
The reason a protocol is needed at all is that a sudden threat triggers a large, fast, involuntary physiological response that specifically impairs the abilities an emergency demands. Sensory information reaching the brain is routed both to the cortex, which analyses it slowly, and to the amygdala, which screens it for threat in something like twelve to twenty milliseconds and can initiate a full response before conscious awareness has formed. The amygdala signals the hypothalamus, which drives the sympathetic nervous system and the adrenal medulla. Within one to three seconds adrenaline and noradrenaline are circulating; within fifteen to thirty minutes cortisol from the slower hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal axis is added on top.

The effects are well characterised and mostly unhelpful for problem-solving. Heart rate rises, sometimes from a resting 70 to over 150 beats per minute within seconds, driven purely by hormones rather than exertion. Blood is shunted from the skin and gut to the large muscles, which is why people go pale and feel sick. Breathing becomes rapid and shallow, often producing hyperventilation that lowers blood carbon dioxide, constricts cerebral blood vessels and causes dizziness, tingling in the hands and lips, and a subjective sense of unreality that people frequently interpret as further evidence that they are in mortal danger.

Perception narrows. Tunnel vision is the best known effect: peripheral visual processing degrades and attention locks onto the perceived threat, so that people genuinely do not see a fire exit, a handhold or an approaching vehicle in their periphery. Auditory exclusion is the equivalent in hearing, and is routinely reported by police officers who did not hear their own gunfire or their partner shouting beside them. Time perception distorts, usually running slow, which appears to be a memory-encoding artefact rather than genuinely accelerated cognition. Pain is suppressed. Fine motor control deteriorates sharply while gross motor performance is maintained or improved, which is why a terrified person can run and lift heroically but cannot tie a knot, operate a zip pull, dial a phone number or manipulate a small buckle.

Various training traditions attach approximate heart-rate bands to these losses, popularised through the work of Bruce Siddle and Dave Grossman, with fine motor skills degrading above roughly 115 beats per minute and complex motor skills and rational cognition above roughly 145. These numbers should be treated as a rough teaching aid rather than a measured law; the underlying impairments are well documented but the specific thresholds are not firmly established, vary hugely between individuals, and depend on whether the heart rate comes from fear or from exercise, which are not equivalent. What is not in doubt is the direction of the effect. The physiological state that a genuine emergency produces is, by design, optimised for fleeing or fighting a predator, and it is actively counterproductive for a situation whose solution requires patience, small hand movements, arithmetic and a map.

sections.heading: What Acute Stress Does to Thinking
sections.body:
The cognitive impairments matter more than the physical ones because they are invisible from the inside. A person with shaking hands knows their hands are shaking. A person whose judgement has narrowed to a single bad option experiences that option as obviously correct.

Working memory shrinks. The ordinary capacity to hold and manipulate perhaps four to seven items at once falls sharply under acute stress, which is why people forget what they were told thirty seconds earlier, cannot retain a grid reference long enough to write it down, and lose track of a sequence of three instructions. Attention narrows in parallel with vision, a phenomenon called cognitive tunnelling. The classic aviation case is Eastern Air Lines Flight 401 in December 1972, in which an entire experienced flight crew became absorbed in a burned-out landing gear indicator bulb while the autopilot quietly descended the aircraft into the Florida Everglades, killing 101 people. Nobody was watching the altimeter. Nobody was incompetent. The attention of every qualified person aboard had converged on one small problem.

Judgement shifts toward the familiar and the recent. Under load, people fall back on whatever response is most practised or was most recently rehearsed, whether or not it fits. They also become markedly worse at revising a belief once formed, a tendency called plan continuation bias or, less politely, get-there-itis. Having decided the car park is over the next rise, the lost walker will cross three rises before entertaining the possibility of being wrong, because each reversal costs something psychologically that the tired stressed brain is unwilling to pay.

Normalcy bias runs the other way and is just as dangerous: the tendency to interpret ambiguous danger signals as ordinary and to continue as normal. It is why people finish their coffee when the fire alarm sounds, why passengers collect hand luggage during an aircraft evacuation, and why residents of a flooding valley wait for a third warning. Related to it is milling, the well-documented behaviour in which people in a threatened crowd seek confirmation from each other rather than acting, standing about, asking questions and watching for someone else to move first. Studies of building evacuations consistently find that the delay before people begin to move is far longer than the movement itself.

Two further effects deserve naming. Hypervigilance is the frantic, unfocused, high-energy state in which a person takes rapid uncoordinated action, tries everything, and finishes exhausted and no further forward; it looks like decisiveness and is the opposite. Its counterpart is freezing, sometimes called tonic immobility, in which action stops entirely. Both are failures of the same regulatory system, and both are precisely what a deliberate protocol is intended to interrupt before it consumes the resources that were the actual margin of survival.

sections.heading: The Ten-Eighty-Ten Pattern and Why Most People Do Nothing
sections.body:
A striking and consistent finding from disaster research is that the majority of people caught in a sudden emergency do not panic, and do not act either. The pattern is often summarised, in a rough and much repeated rule of thumb, as ten, eighty, ten: roughly ten per cent of people respond quickly and effectively; roughly eighty per cent become stunned, docile and passive, waiting to be told what to do; and roughly ten per cent behave in genuinely counterproductive ways, including uncontrolled panic, screaming, inappropriate aggression or paralysis. The proportions are impressionistic rather than measured and vary with the type of event, so the figures should be held loosely, but the underlying shape has been replicated across shipwrecks, fires, earthquakes, aircraft accidents and terrorist incidents.

The eighty per cent are the interesting group. The psychologist John Leach, who has studied survival behaviour extensively, describes this state as a form of cognitive paralysis in which the brain is searching for a behavioural template that matches the situation and, finding none, produces no output at all. People in it describe being aware, being able to see and hear, and being unable to decide. They can, crucially, follow instructions. This is why loud, specific, directive commands are so effective in evacuations, and why the single most useful thing a bystander can do is name a person and give them one concrete task.

The most commonly cited illustration is the popular account of the 1977 Tenerife airport disaster, in which two Boeing 747s collided on the runway and 583 people died. Survivors from the Pan Am aircraft, which was not immediately destroyed, later described passengers sitting still in their seats while the cabin filled with smoke, some apparently uninjured, until fire reached them; those who lived were largely people who unbuckled and moved within the first seconds. Similar behaviour has been recorded repeatedly, from the 1985 Manchester airport fire to the evacuation of the World Trade Center in 2001, where the average delay before occupants began to descend has been estimated in the several-minute range.

The practical lesson is twofold and slightly uncomfortable. First, the default human response to sudden catastrophe is not heroism or hysteria but a kind of blank compliance, and you should assume it will happen to you unless you have deliberately trained otherwise. Second, membership of the effective ten per cent is not primarily a matter of courage or temperament. Research on survivors repeatedly points to prior mental rehearsal, familiarity with the environment, and possession of a simple pre-decided procedure as the distinguishing features. People who had thought about it beforehand acted; people who had not, waited. A protocol such as STOP is valuable largely because it is a template you can install in advance, so that when the brain searches for a matching behaviour there is at least one available.

sections.heading: S is for Stop: Interrupting the Action Loop
sections.body:
The first step is the one people resist hardest and the one that does most of the work. It means physically stopping: ceasing all movement and all task activity, immediately, for a defined period. Not slowing down, not continuing while thinking, not carrying on until the top of the next rise. Stop.

There are three reasons this is not merely symbolic. The first is that further motion in an unknown direction actively worsens most situations. A person who realises they are lost is, at that instant, closer to their last known position than they will ever be again, and the last known position is what searchers will work outward from. Statistical analysis of search and rescue incidents consistently finds most subjects within a few kilometres of the point where they were last confirmed, so every additional kilometre of uninformed movement expands the search area roughly with the square of the distance and makes an already difficult problem geometrically harder. The same logic applies to a diver, a boat crew, a caver and a driver in a whiteout.

The second is that stopping is the physical act that breaks the escalating feedback between action and arousal. Movement in a frightened state feeds arousal, arousal narrows attention, narrowed attention produces worse decisions, which produce more fright. Interrupting the motor component interrupts the cycle. The traditional instruction is more specific than merely halting: sit down. Sitting is difficult to do in a state of hypervigilance, which is exactly why it works as a circuit-breaker. It also reduces the chance of falling, which is a real risk on steep ground with adrenaline running and fine control degraded.

The third reason is that a fixed pause converts an open-ended emotional state into a bounded, manageable task. Various traditions attach a nominal duration: sit for at least fifteen minutes, or count sixty slow breaths, or in aviation the discipline of doing nothing for the first few seconds beyond flying the aircraft. The exact number matters less than having one. Fifteen minutes is a reasonable default for a wilderness situation; it is long enough for adrenaline levels to begin dropping noticeably and short enough that it does not feel like surrender.

Two practical points make the stop more effective. Do something small, physical and constructive with your hands while stopped: put on a layer of clothing, drink water, eat a little food, sit on your pack rather than on wet ground. This addresses real physiological needs, occupies the hands, and gives the pause a purpose that feels less like doing nothing. And say it out loud. Verbalising, whether alone or to a group, engages language processing and helps break the wordless loop. In a group, one person saying we are stopping for fifteen minutes gives everyone else the permission that eighty per cent of them are waiting for.

sections.heading: T is for Think: Deliberate Reasoning Instead of Reflex
sections.body:
Having stopped, the task is to restart the slow, deliberate, effortful kind of thinking that stress has suppressed, in place of the fast, automatic, associative kind that is now running unchecked. The distinction corresponds to what Daniel Kahneman popularised as System 1 and System 2, and while that framing is a simplification of a contested area of psychology, it captures the practical point exactly: the fast system is still running and it is producing confident answers, and those answers are not to be trusted right now.

The first thing to think about is not the problem. It is your own state. Ask deliberately whether you are breathing fast, whether your hands are shaking, whether you feel unreal or dizzy, whether you are angry. Naming an emotional state has a measurable regulatory effect, an idea supported by neuroimaging work by Matthew Lieberman and colleagues showing that putting feelings into words is associated with reduced amygdala activity. Saying to yourself, plainly, I am frightened and my judgement is currently unreliable, is not weakness; it is the single most useful piece of intelligence available at that moment, and it is the reason the second step exists rather than jumping straight to observation.

The second thing to think about is what is actually urgent, and the honest answer is usually far less than it feels. Almost every non-medical emergency permits several minutes of thought without material worsening. The traditional way of grounding this is the rule of threes, a rough mnemonic that a person can survive roughly three minutes without air, three hours without shelter in a hostile environment, three days without water and three weeks without food. The numbers are approximations, vary enormously with conditions and should not be treated as promises, but they impose a useful priority order that is frequently the opposite of what panic suggests. A lost walker's instinct is to worry about food and about getting home; the actual threats, in order, are the cliff in the dark, the cold night and the empty water bottle.

The third thing to think about is what you actually know for certain and where the boundary of your knowledge lies. Distinguish observation from inference. You know that you have not seen a waymark for forty minutes; you do not know that the path is behind you. You know that the tide is coming in; you do not know that the cove has no exit. Under stress people convert assumptions into facts within seconds and then reason from them confidently, and the discipline of asking how do I know that is one of the few reliable defences.

Finally, think about time. Note the current time explicitly. Work out how many hours of daylight remain. Almost every subsequent decision depends on that number, and it is remarkably easy in a stressed state to spend two hours on something without noticing that the light has gone.

sections.heading: O is for Observe: Building an Accurate Picture
sections.body:
Observation is deliberate, systematic evidence-gathering, and it is where the protocol earns most of its practical value. The stressed mind samples the environment badly, fixating on the threat and ignoring everything else, so the fix is to impose an order and work through it whether or not each item feels relevant. The habit of running the same sweep every time is what stops you skipping the item that mattered.

Start with yourself and anyone with you. Are you injured, and how badly? Are you bleeding, and from where? People in the first minutes of an incident frequently do not notice significant injuries, so run a hands-on check rather than relying on how you feel. Are you cold, wet, dehydrated, exhausted, hypoglycaemic? Each of these degrades judgement further and each has a cheap remedy that should be applied now rather than later. Then check the others in your party in the same order, out loud, by name.

Then the environment. What is the weather doing and what is it about to do? How much daylight is left, specifically, in hours? What is the terrain immediately around you and what does it prevent? Where is water? Where is shelter, natural or otherwise? What can you hear, which in poor visibility is often more informative than what you can see: a road, a river, surf, livestock, aircraft, a generator. Where is the wind coming from, which governs smoke, scent, wind chill and fire behaviour.

Then position. What was the last point you are certain of, and how long ago? What direction have you travelled since, and at roughly what speed? A walking pace of four to five kilometres per hour on a good path, two to three on rough ground and under one in dense brush or deep snow lets you convert elapsed time into a distance estimate, which combined with a compass bearing gives a usable position circle even without a map fix. Note landmarks with known bearings. If a map and compass are available, take a resection from two or three identifiable features.

Then resources, and this step is done physically. Empty the pack and pockets and lay everything out where you can see it. People consistently forget what they are carrying under stress, and an item that goes unremembered might as well not exist. Note water and food quantity, insulation, waterproofs, light and spare batteries, fire-lighting, cutting tools, cordage, first aid, signalling equipment, phone battery percentage and signal state, and anything improvisable. A survival blanket, a whistle and a head torch in a side pocket change the entire calculation.

Finally, observe the human system beyond yourself. Does anyone know where you went and when you were due back? Has a search been triggered, or will one be, and when? Is there phone or radio coverage anywhere nearby, perhaps higher up? Are there other people within reach? The answer to whether anyone is coming for you changes the correct plan more than almost anything else, because it determines whether the objective is to be found or to self-rescue.

sections.heading: P is for Plan: Choosing Something You Can Actually Do
sections.body:
Planning turns observations into a course of action, and the commonest error is to skip straight here from the initial shock, which produces a plan built on assumptions rather than evidence. A plan made properly has a small number of recognisable properties, and it is worth checking them explicitly rather than trusting the feeling of having decided.

It should address the priorities in the right order. Immediate life threats first, then protection from the environment, then water, then signalling and navigation, then food, then comfort. This ordering repeatedly surprises people because it demotes the thing they are most emotionally focused on, which is usually getting home. Cold kills people who were three hours from a road; nobody in a temperate country has starved to death during a weekend.

It should be executable with what you actually have, in the time and light available, at your current level of capability. A plan requiring a two-hour traverse with ninety minutes of daylight left is not a plan. A plan requiring fine manipulation from someone whose hands are numb needs to be reordered so the fiddly work happens after warming up. Be explicit about the resource you are spending, whether that is daylight, battery, water, warmth or physical reserve, because most emergencies are ultimately budget problems.

It should have a stated goal, a first concrete action and a decision point. Vagueness is where plans fail. Compare head roughly downhill and hope with the following: walk on a bearing of 140 degrees for one hour to reach the stream, follow it downstream, and if no track is found within two hours from now, stop and build a shelter while there is still light. The second version is testable. It contains a trigger that tells you when the plan has failed, which the stressed mind will otherwise never generate on its own, and it protects the single most perishable resource, daylight.

It should be conservative about irreversibility. Prefer actions you can undo.
