The most widely taught is START, Simple Triage And Rapid Treatment, developed in Newport Beach, California, in 1983 by Hoag Hospital and the local fire department. It begins by calling out an instruction for anyone able to walk to move to a designated area; everyone who walks is tagged green immediately, which typically removes most of the casualties from the problem in under a minute. The remaining non-ambulatory casualties are assessed on three checks, in order. Respiration: if not breathing, open the airway once; if breathing starts, tag red; if not, tag black. If the respiratory rate is above 30 per minute, tag red. Perfusion: check the radial pulse or capillary refill; absent radial pulse, or capillary refill over two seconds, means red, and control any major bleeding at that moment. Mental status: if the casualty cannot follow a simple command, tag red. Anyone passing all three is yellow.

The British and much of the Commonwealth use the Triage Sieve, which is similar in structure but uses slightly different cut-offs — respiratory rate under 10 or over 29, and a capillary refill over two seconds or a pulse over 120 — and is followed later by a more detailed Triage Sort using the Glasgow Coma Scale, respiratory rate and systolic blood pressure to produce a Revised Trauma Score. JumpSTART is the paediatric variant, necessary because children compensate differently: their normal respiratory rates are higher, and a child in respiratory arrest with a pulse may respond to five rescue breaths, so JumpSTART includes that step where adult START does not. SALT — Sort, Assess, Lifesaving interventions, Treatment and transport — is a more recent American system that adds a step for a few immediate interventions during the sort itself.

Two design features are worth noticing because they generalise. First, the systems front-load the cheapest discriminator: asking people to walk costs nothing and resolves the majority of cases. Second, they deliberately accept error in exchange for speed. START is known to over-triage, tagging people red who turn out not to need it, at rates that in some studies exceed 50 percent. That is a designed-in bias, because under-triage — missing someone who needed immediate care — kills, whereas over-triage merely wastes effort. Where the two errors have asymmetric costs, the rule should be biased toward the cheaper error.

sections.heading: The lifesaving interventions permitted during sorting
sections.body:
A tension sits at the heart of every sorting system: the person doing the triage must keep moving, yet some casualties will die in the next two minutes from something that takes fifteen seconds to fix. The resolution adopted by essentially all modern systems is a very short, explicitly enumerated list of interventions permitted during the sort. Anything on the list is done immediately and the responder moves on. Anything not on the list waits for the treatment phase, however tempting it is.

The list is short because each item satisfies three tests: it takes seconds rather than minutes, it requires no equipment beyond what the responder carries, and it addresses a cause of death that is both rapid and reversible. Opening an airway is the first — a simple head-tilt chin-lift, or a jaw thrust where spinal injury is suspected, or rolling an unconscious breathing casualty into the recovery position so the tongue and vomit do not obstruct. Airway obstruction kills within minutes and the fix is free.

Controlling catastrophic external haemorrhage is the second, and modern practice has moved it to the top. A person with a severed femoral artery can exsanguinate in three to five minutes. A windlass tourniquet applied high and tight on a limb takes about 20 to 30 seconds, and haemostatic gauze packed firmly into a junctional wound takes a little longer. Military experience in Iraq and Afghanistan drove this change: tourniquets, long discouraged in civilian practice out of fear of limb loss, were shown to save lives with far lower complication rates than had been assumed, and the modern consensus is that a tourniquet can safely remain in place for around two hours and often considerably longer. This is why the current mnemonic in tactical and increasingly in civilian care is not ABC but MARCH — Massive haemorrhage, Airway, Respiration, Circulation, Hypothermia — putting bleeding before airway because it kills faster.

Decompressing a tension pneumothorax with a needle is on the list where the responder is trained and equipped, since it takes seconds and reverses an otherwise fatal spiral. In chemical incidents, administering an antidote auto-injector is included for the same reason.

What is deliberately excluded is as instructive as what is included. Cardiopulmonary resuscitation is not performed during mass-casualty triage. In a normal setting CPR is correct; in a mass-casualty setting it commits one or two responders entirely to a casualty whose survival odds after traumatic arrest are very low, while others with far better prospects go untreated. Spinal immobilisation, splinting, wound dressing, intravenous access and detailed examination all wait. Responders find this extremely difficult, and the discipline of walking past someone in obvious distress to reach someone quieter and more salvageable is the hardest habit the training has to install.

sections.heading: Reverse triage, and how the objective changes the answer
sections.body:
The rule "treat the worst first" and the rule "treat the most salvageable first" give different answers, and which is correct depends entirely on what is being optimised. Making that objective explicit is the single most clarifying act in any triage decision, and failing to do so produces most of the confused arguments about the subject.

In ordinary emergency medicine with adequate resources, the objective is the individual patient's outcome, and the sickest is treated first. In a mass-casualty incident the objective is aggregate survival, and the most salvageable is treated first. In military triage a third objective enters: preserving fighting strength, which can mean prioritising the lightly wounded who can return to duty within hours over the severely wounded who cannot. This is called reverse triage, and it is a genuine and long-standing military doctrine rather than a euphemism. The North Africa penicillin decision of 1943 is its clearest historical illustration.

Reverse triage also appears in civilian settings under a different name. During a hospital surge — a pandemic, a mass shooting, an earthquake — hospitals perform reverse triage by identifying existing inpatients who can be discharged early with acceptable risk, in order to free beds for incoming casualties. The objective there is system capacity rather than any individual outcome.

A fourth objective, distinct again, is the survival of the responding group itself. In wilderness, maritime, mountain and disaster settings the rule "do not create additional casualties" outranks all treatment priorities. A rescuer who enters a confined space filled with hydrogen sulphide to reach a collapsed colleague usually becomes the second body; this pattern is so consistent in confined-space and grain-entrapment fatalities that the multiple-fatality outcome is the expected one. Scene safety first is not timidity, it is triage applied to the rescue capability itself, treating the responder as the scarcest and most valuable resource present.

The practical consequence is that before applying any algorithm you must answer one question: what am I trying to maximise? Total lives saved? Lives saved among a specific group I am responsible for? The capability to continue operating? The survival of the person I love, at the cost of strangers? That last one is not a hypothetical — it is what people actually do, and pretending otherwise makes the framework useless in real families and real small groups. An honest treatment of triage acknowledges that the utilitarian aggregate objective is a choice, defensible in a public-service role where you act on behalf of everyone, and not obviously binding on a private individual acting for their own family. Different objectives are legitimate in different roles; what is never legitimate is having no objective and therefore making inconsistent decisions that serve none of them.

sections.heading: Triage applied to yourself and to a small group
sections.body:
Most people who ever need triage thinking will not be sorting fifty strangers. They will be one of three or four people in a vehicle after a crash, on a mountain in deteriorating weather, or in a house after an earthquake, and the sorting problem is small, personal and immediate. The same structure applies, and it can be run in about a minute.

Start with yourself. This feels selfish and it is not: an injured helper is a second casualty and a subtracted rescuer, and the sequence for a group of four with one injured person is entirely different from a group of two with two injured. Check for catastrophic bleeding on your own body — run hands over torso, groin, armpits and limbs, then look at them, because adrenaline reliably masks pain and people have walked considerable distances on open fractures and deep lacerations without noticing. Confirm you can breathe, see and think clearly. Only then look outward.

Next, count. Establish how many people there are, how many are moving and talking, and how many are not. The single loudest casualty is usually not the sickest, because screaming requires an airway, breathing and enough perfusion to be conscious. The quiet ones need looking at first. This inversion is counterintuitive and it is the most useful single heuristic in small-group triage.

Then assess capacity honestly. What do you actually have — hands, hours of daylight, warmth, a phone with signal, a vehicle, a first aid kit, water? Capacity determines categories. With a helicopter twenty minutes out, almost everyone is salvageable and the job is to keep them alive until it lands. With a two-day walk to the nearest road in worsening weather, the calculus changes completely and hard choices arrive quickly.

Finally, decide and commit. The most common failure in small groups is not choosing wrongly but oscillating — starting to help one person, moving to another when they cry out, going back, and accomplishing nothing for anyone. Set a plan aloud, assign named people to specific jobs, and stick with it until new information genuinely changes the picture. Speaking decisions aloud does three things at once: it forces you to make them explicit, it lets others correct an error, and it gives frightened people something to do, which is itself stabilising.

Keep re-checking as you go. In a group of four, the picture changes fast: a person who was walking and talking may sit down and go quiet, which is exactly the pattern of internal bleeding declaring itself. Make a habit of looking at everyone every few minutes, not only the person you are working on.

One further point specific to small groups: you will know these people. The framework says treat by salvageability and you will want to treat by love. Decide before the moment which rule you intend to follow, because deciding in the moment, with someone you care about bleeding in front of you, is not a decision anyone makes well.

sections.heading: The wider application: resources, tasks and attention
sections.body:
The reason triage belongs among foundational concepts rather than in a first-aid manual is that its structure — scarce resource, competing claims, an explicit rule, asymmetric costs of error — describes an enormous range of situations that have nothing to do with injuries. Once the pattern is visible, it becomes a general tool for thinking under constraint.

Consider resource triage. A stranded group has four litres of water, some food, one lighter and a half-charged phone. The naive approach is to ration everything equally and gradually. The triage approach asks which shortage kills first and allocates accordingly. The rough survival envelope — three minutes without air, three hours without shelter in hostile weather, three days without water, three weeks without food — is crude and much criticised, since a person can survive far longer than three hours in mild conditions and far less than three minutes in cold water, but its value is as an ordering, not a set of durations. It says shelter usually outranks water, water almost always outranks food, and that spending the last daylight hour foraging while lacking any protection from a freezing night is a categorical error. Hypothermia kills healthy people in temperate conditions astonishingly fast, and it is the classic case of a group triaging for the wrong shortage.

Consider task triage. When five things need doing and there is time for two, the correct discriminators are which task has a deadline that will pass, which task unlocks other tasks, and which task fails irreversibly. Building shelter before dark has a hard deadline; digging a latrine does not. Signalling while an aircraft is overhead is irreversible if missed. The tasks that appear urgent because they are noisy or emotionally pressing are frequently the ones that can wait.

Consider attention triage, which is the version most people meet daily. Attention is genuinely finite; the demands on it are effectively infinite; and the failure mode is identical to the small-group oscillation problem — attending to whatever is loudest, achieving partial progress everywhere and completion nowhere. The same corrective applies: name the objective, sort by consequence rather than by volume, commit, and re-sort only when real new information arrives.

Consider also organisational and technical triage, where the term is used almost unchanged. Engineers triage bugs, hospitals triage waiting lists, aid agencies triage villages, and in each case the same three failure modes recur: no explicit objective, sorting by whoever complains loudest, and refusing to place anything in the lowest category. That last refusal is the commonest and most damaging, because a system in which nothing is ever deprioritised has not made a decision at all; it has merely distributed its scarcity randomly and called that fairness.

sections.heading: Over-triage, under-triage and the cost of error
sections.body:
Every sorting system makes mistakes, and the two kinds of mistake are not symmetric. Under-triage means assigning a casualty to a lower category than their condition warrants — sending someone home who has a slowly expanding subdural haematoma, or tagging yellow a patient with a tension pneumothorax that has not yet declared itself. Under-triage kills directly, and the deaths are attributable and visible in retrospect.

Over-triage means assigning a higher category than warranted, and its cost is indirect: resources consumed on people who did not need them, and therefore unavailable for those who did. In small incidents over-triage is nearly free, which is why deliberately conservative systems are correct there. In large incidents it becomes lethal at scale. The most-cited evidence comes from analyses of terrorist bombings, where a strong relationship has been observed between over-triage rate and the mortality of the critically injured: hospitals overwhelmed with lightly injured patients arriving first and being worked up as priorities delivered worse outcomes for the genuinely critical. Figures around a doubling of critical mortality at high over-triage rates are commonly quoted from this literature, and while the exact numbers depend on the events analysed and are debated, the direction of the effect is well established.

The practical response is to accept a designed asymmetry and to state it. Most field systems accept over-triage rates of 30 to 50 percent as the price of keeping under-triage near 5 percent or below. That is a deliberate trade, not sloppiness. Where the resource is genuinely, hard-limited — one ventilator, one surgeon, one helicopter seat — the trade shifts and precision matters more, which is why hospital-level triage uses slower, more accurate scoring than field triage does.

Two systematic biases distort real triage and both are worth knowing by name. The first is the tendency to over-prioritise dramatic-looking injuries: an amputated hand or a badly burned face is horrifying and often not immediately life-threatening, while a quiet abdomen filling with blood looks like nothing. Visual salience and lethality are only loosely related. The second is anchoring on the first assessment. A casualty tagged yellow tends to stay yellow even as they deteriorate, because subsequent responders read the tag rather than the patient. This is why systematic re-triage at every stage is mandatory in all serious systems and why tags are designed to be updated rather than replaced.

A third error is subtler: refusing to use the lowest category at all. A responder who cannot bring themselves to designate anyone expectant will spend disproportionate resources on the unsalvageable, and the deaths that result are diffuse, delayed and unattributable — which is precisely what makes this failure so persistent. It feels like compassion and functions as harm.

sections.heading: Ethics: what fairness means when there is not enough
sections.body:
Triage is applied ethics under time pressure, and the philosophical positions it draws on are genuinely in conflict rather than merely differing in emphasis. The dominant framework is utilitarian: maximise total benefit, usually counted as lives saved or life-years saved. It has the great virtue of being computable and the great vice of being willing, in principle, to sacrifice an individual entirely for aggregate gain. A deontological objection holds that each person has a claim to care that cannot simply be summed away, and that a system treating people as units of expected benefit has stopped treating them as people. Egalitarian approaches argue that where claims are comparable, the only fair allocation is a genuine lottery, because any substantive criterion smuggles in a judgement about whose life is worth more.

Real allocation policies mix these. Most published frameworks agree on excluding certain criteria absolutely: ability to pay, social status, celebrity, race, religion, nationality, and — with important qualifications — disability. The disability question is the sharpest live controversy. A criterion like expected life-years saved, applied mechanically, systematically disadvantages disabled and chronically ill people even when their prospect of surviving the acute episode is identical. Disability rights advocates have argued, with considerable force and some legal success, that this constitutes discrimination; several allocation protocols drafted early in the COVID-19 pandemic were revised or withdrawn after such challenges. There is no settled resolution, and anyone presenting one is overstating the state of the argument.

Age is similarly contested. The fair-innings argument holds that a person who has already had a long life has less claim on a scarce resource than one who has not, and it has real intuitive pull. Against it stands the objection that this is straightforward age discrimination and that it treats a life already lived as reducing a person's present worth. Most frameworks use age only as a clinical prognostic factor rather than as an independent tie-breaker, which is a compromise rather than a solution.

Lotteries deserve a word of their own, because they are more defensible than they first appear. Where two claimants genuinely cannot be distinguished on prognosis, a random draw treats them as equals in a way that no substantive criterion can, and it removes the opportunity for bias to enter under the cover of clinical judgement. Its weakness is that it feels arbitrary to everyone involved and is very hard for a clinician to explain to a family.

A few procedural principles command wide agreement and are worth holding onto because they survive disagreement about the substance. Criteria should be decided in advance, not invented in the moment, because decisions made under pressure drift toward whoever is present and articulate. They should be public, so they can be criticised. They should be applied consistently to everyone including the decision-makers and their families. And, importantly, the person making allocation decisions should ideally not be the person providing bedside care to a specific patient, because the two roles pull in opposite directions and holding both is corrosive. Hospitals implementing crisis standards separate the triage officer from the treating clinician for exactly this reason.

sections.heading: Crisis standards of care beyond the battlefield
sections.body:
The most consequential recent expansion of triage thinking has been into civilian health systems facing sustained rather than momentary scarcity. Mass-casualty triage assumes a surge lasting hours; crisis standards of care address scarcity lasting weeks or months, and the ethical and practical problems are different because the decisions are repeated, documented and made by institutions rather than by individuals in the field.

The framework was developed in the United States largely through Institute of Medicine work published in 2009 and 2012, prompted by pandemic influenza planning and by the experience of Hurricane Katrina, and parallel frameworks exist in many countries. It describes a continuum: conventional care, where normal standards apply; contingency care, where functionally equivalent substitutions are made, such as using a recovery room as an intensive care bay; and crisis care, where standards genuinely fall and allocation decisions must be made. The transition into crisis standards is meant to be a formal, declared, accountable act by a designated authority rather than something that happens quietly ward by ward, precisely so that the decisions are visible and reviewable.

The COVID-19 pandemic tested this extensively and revealed a gap between planning and practice. Northern Italy in March 2020, New York in April 2020, and later India and Brazil, all experienced periods where demand for oxygen, ventilators or beds exceeded supply. Published protocols typically used the Sequential Organ Failure Assessment score as a prognostic tool, sometimes with tie-breakers based on short-term survival or on a lottery, and often with a rule that a patient allocated a ventilator would be reassessed at fixed intervals and could have it withdrawn if not improving. That last provision is legally and psychologically explosive — withdrawing a treatment already started is experienced very differently from never starting it, though most ethicists argue there is no morally relevant distinction — and it was among the least implemented parts of the protocols.

Crisis standards also reach beyond intensive care. Scarcity during that period showed up as shortages of oxygen cylinders, dialysis capacity, blood products, staff, and in some places something as mundane as functioning transport, and each of those required its own allocation rule. The general lesson is that the binding constraint is often not the one the plan anticipated, and a framework that can only ration ventilators is of limited use when what has actually run out is nurses.

Several honest lessons emerged. Formal protocols were frequently not invoked even where scarcity was real, because declaring crisis standards is politically costly and clinicians preferred to make informal bedside decisions. Informal decisions proved less consistent and less defensible. Advance planning was worth far more than in-the-moment ethics. And triage of a scarce resource is only ever a second-best response: every hour spent expanding supply, sharing load between hospitals, transferring patients or improvising equipment removed the need to ration at all. The general principle is important and applies everywhere. Triage is what you do when you have failed, or been unable, to increase capacity, and the first response to scarcity should always be an attempt to make the scarcity go away.

sections.heading: Running a triage: a working sequence
sections.body:
This is the sequence for a lightly trained person arriving at an incident with multiple casualties and no professional help present — a road collision, a building collapse, a group accident in remote country — where you are the most capable person available. If professionals are present, report what you found and follow their direction.

The most important instruction is the first one, and it is the one people skip. A dead rescuer converts a bad situation into a worse one.
steps: Stop before entering and assess the hazard. Traffic, fire, fuel, unstable structure, electricity, water, gas, gunfire, animals, and confined-space atmospheres all kill responders. If you cannot make the scene safe, do not enter; call for help and keep others out. This decision is triage applied to the scarcest resource present, which is you.

Call for help before treating anyone, and give a structured report: exact location, what happened, approximate number of casualties, hazards present, and what you need. On a satellite messenger or a poor phone line, send location and casualty count first — those are the two facts that determine the response.

Call out loudly: anyone who can walk, come to me here. Direct them to a single safe spot and tag them green. This clears the majority of casualties in under a minute and identifies people who can help.

Recruit from the green group immediately. Assign specific named tasks: one person to meet emergency services, one to hold pressure on a bleeding wound, two to fetch blankets and insulation, one to keep a count of casualties. Vague requests achieve nothing; specific assignments to named people work.

Move through the remaining casualties in a systematic pattern — one side to the other, or a spiral outward — spending no more than 30 to 60 seconds on each. Do not backtrack toward whoever is loudest.

For each casualty check three things in order. Are they breathing? If not, open the airway once; if breathing starts they are red, if not they are black. Is there catastrophic bleeding? Apply a tourniquet or firm pressure now. Can they follow a simple instruction such as squeeze my hand?

Tag each casualty visibly and move on. Do not stop to dress wounds, splint fractures, immobilise spines or begin CPR during the sorting pass; each of these commits you to one person and abandons the rest.
When the sweep is complete you have a picture. Now return and treat, working through the red group first, then yellow, using the green group's hands to multiply your own.

Protect everyone from the ground and the weather. Hypothermia kills injured people in conditions a healthy person finds mild, because injury, blood loss and immobility all destroy thermoregulation. Insulation underneath matters more than covering on top.

Re-triage continuously. Casualties deteriorate and improve, and categories change when help or transport arrives. Re-check the yellow group especially, since that is where deterioration is most often missed.

Hand over properly when professionals arrive: number of casualties, categories assigned, interventions performed and when, and anything that has changed. A clear thirty-second handover beats another ten minutes of your own treatment.

sections.heading: Marking, recording and communicating the sort
sections.body:
A triage decision that nobody else can read is worth very little, because the whole point of sorting is to direct the effort of other people, most of whom will arrive after you and know nothing of what you found. Marking is therefore not administration; it is the mechanism by which the sort actually changes behaviour.

Formal triage tags are printed cards, usually with tear-off coloured strips so that a casualty can be downgraded by tearing to a new colour, a unique serial number, space for injuries, interventions and times, and often a detachable stub for the incident log. Systems such as METTAG and SMART tags dominate professional practice. The serial number matters more than people expect: in a large incident with casualties dispersed to several hospitals, the number is often the only way to reconcile who went where, and unidentified casualties are a persistent problem in real disasters.

Improvised marking works well provided it is unambiguous and visible from a distance. Write directly on the casualty's forehead or the back of a hand with a permanent marker — a practice used in real disasters because paper is lost and skin is not. Record the category letter, the time, and any tourniquet application, since a tourniquet applied and then hidden under a blanket has caused avoidable limb loss; the convention is a large T and the time written on the forehead. Coloured tape, cloth strips, cable ties or torn plastic bags tied to a wrist or ankle all serve. Whatever you use, use one system consistently and tell arriving responders what it means in the first sentence of your handover.

Keep a written casualty count somewhere that is not your memory. Under stress, people reliably lose count, and the number of casualties is the single most important figure the incoming response needs, because it determines how many ambulances, how many crews and which hospitals are activated. A tally scratched on a car bonnet in the dust is adequate.
ingredients: Commercial triage tags with tear-off colour strips and serial numbers, if available; a pack of fifty weighs little and lives in a vehicle or group kit.
A permanent marker with a broad tip, which writes on skin, tape, plastic and wet surfaces. This is the single most useful marking item and costs almost nothing.
Coloured tape or ribbon in red, yellow, green and black, or any four visually distinct colours agreed in advance. Electrical tape, surveyor's flagging tape and torn fabric all work.
A notebook and pencil, or any writable surface. Pencil writes in rain and cold where most pens fail.
A means of calling for help that does not depend on mobile coverage where coverage is unreliable: a satellite messenger, a radio, a whistle, or a signalling mirror.
A watch, because interventions must be timed. The time a tourniquet went on is clinically important information and is easily lost.

sections.heading: The psychological cost, and how people are trained to bear it
sections.body:
Triage imposes a specific kind of harm on the person performing it, and any treatment of the subject that omits this is incomplete. The relevant concept is moral injury: distress arising not from fear for one's own safety but from having done, or failed to prevent, something that violates one's own moral code. It is distinct from post-traumatic stress disorder in origin, though the two frequently co-occur, and it is characteristically accompanied by guilt and shame rather than fear. The term was developed in work with military veterans by Jonathan Shay and later by Brett Litz and colleagues, and it has since been applied extensively to healthcare workers, particularly after the COVID-19 pandemic, where clinicians describing the experience of rationing care reported exactly this pattern.

The predictable flashpoints are known. Assigning someone to an expectant category and then walking past them while they are still conscious. Choosing between two casualties knowing that the one not chosen will probably die. Being unable to reach someone audible but inaccessible. Making a decision under uncertainty that later evidence shows was wrong. Being praised afterwards for actions you privately regard as failures. Notably, the distress is often worst in those who performed best, because competent people continue to analyse the decision afterwards.

Several protective factors are reasonably well supported. Training that has rehearsed the decision in advance reduces both hesitation at the time and self-blame afterwards, because the decision is experienced as applying a system rather than as a personal choice. Explicit team structure helps for the same reason, distributing the decision. Debriefing that is factual and blame-free, conducted soon afterwards, helps; single-session psychological debriefing of the older mandated kind has been found in reviews to be ineffective and possibly harmful, so the current emphasis is on peer support, monitoring, and access to proper treatment for those who need it rather than on compulsory group processing.

Rehearsal is the practical intervention available to almost anyone. Reading about a decision is not the same as having made one, and the value of tabletop exercises, simulated casualty scenarios and even mentally walking through a specific incident on a specific road is that they convert a novel horror into a recognised pattern. Professional responders drill mass-casualty scenarios repeatedly for this reason, and the effect is not that they stop feeling anything but that the feeling arrives after the work rather than during it.

Three things are worth saying plainly to anyone who has had to do this. First, the guilt is a sign of intact moral sense, not of wrongdoing. Second, outcomes are a poor guide to decision quality: a good decision under uncertainty can produce a bad result, and judging yourself on the result rather than on what you knew at the time is both unfair and unhelpful. Third, the counterfactual is almost never the one that guilt proposes. The mind offers the fantasy that everyone could have been saved with better choices; the honest comparison is against what would have happened had nobody sorted at all, which is usually more deaths, not fewer.

sections.heading: Limits of the concept and honest uncertainty
sections.body:
Triage is a useful framework with real boundaries, and knowing where it stops being useful is part of understanding it. The first limit is evidential. Field triage systems are, by the nature of the situations they are used in, extremely difficult to study; there are almost no randomised trials, the literature relies heavily on retrospective analyses of individual disasters and on simulation exercises, and comparisons between systems have generally failed to show one clearly superior to another. START, SIEVE, SALT and their relatives are best understood as reasonable, internally consistent conventions rather than as empirically optimised algorithms. Anyone claiming a definitive accuracy figure for a triage system should be read sceptically.

The second limit is prognostic. Triage depends on predicting who will survive with treatment and who will not, and that prediction is unreliable at the individual level. People categorised expectant have survived; people categorised yellow have died within the hour. Trauma scoring systems perform respectably across populations and poorly for the single patient in front of you. Head injury is particularly treacherous, since a patient who is talking now may have an expanding intracranial bleed, and hypothermic casualties can appear dead and recover fully — the maxim that a hypothermia victim is not dead until warm and dead is genuinely correct, and cold-water drowning survivals after well over half an hour of submersion are documented.

The third limit is that triage assumes fixed resources, which is often false. Its correct place is downstream of every attempt to enlarge capacity: recruiting bystanders, improvising equipment, calling in more help, moving casualties to where resources are, or simply waiting where waiting is safe. A group that begins rationing without first asking whether the scarcity can be removed has skipped the more valuable step.

The fourth limit is scope creep. The utilitarian logic that is appropriate under acute scarcity becomes corrosive when applied where scarcity does not actually bind. Treating ordinary life as a permanent triage, in which people and obligations are constantly ranked by expected return, is not rigorous thinking; it is a category error that borrows the moral licence of an emergency for situations that do not warrant it.

A fifth limit is cultural and legal. Triage frameworks were largely written in wealthy countries with functioning emergency systems, and they assume things that are not universally true: that transport exists, that a hospital will accept whoever arrives, and that families will accept a stranger's authority to sort their relatives. Where one of those assumptions fails, a system that ignores the local reality will simply be overridden by it.

The final and least comfortable limit is that triage does not produce good outcomes. It produces the least bad outcome available given a situation that has already gone wrong. It cannot restore what has been lost, and it offers no consolation. Its entire claim is that systematic allocation under scarcity kills fewer people than allocation by instinct, sympathy or proximity — a claim that is well supported and that remains, when everything has been said, a bleak thing to be right about.

sections.heading: When it goes wrong, and what to do afterwards
sections.body:
Triage fails in a small number of recognisable ways, and knowing them makes them recoverable. The most common is paralysis: the responder freezes, unable to choose, and treats nobody. The corrective is mechanical — start the algorithm rather than the decision. Call out for anyone who can walk. Ask the first non-walking casualty whether they are breathing. Once the sequence is running, it carries you, which is precisely why crude algorithms exist.

The second is fixation, in which a responder attaches to one casualty — often the youngest, the loudest, or someone they know — and spends the entire incident on them. It is recognised by looking up and realising you have no idea how many casualties there are. The corrective is a hard rule set in advance: complete the sweep before beginning any treatment, and have someone else say aloud when your time on one person exceeds a minute.

The third is over-triage collapse, where everyone has been tagged red and the categories have therefore conveyed nothing. If more than roughly a third of casualties are red, re-sort with stricter criteria; a system that discriminates nothing is worse than none, because it consumes time while providing false confidence.

The fourth is losing the count and the record. If you no longer know how many casualties there are or what you did to whom, stop and rebuild the picture before doing anything else, then hand over what you actually know rather than what you assume. Overstating certainty in a handover is far more damaging than admitting a gap.

Afterwards, three things matter and they are usually done badly. Hand over completely, including the decisions you are unsure about; the incoming team can revise a category, but only if they know it exists. Record what happened while it is fresh — times, categories, interventions — because memory degrades quickly and because reviews conducted months later depend on contemporaneous notes. And review the incident factually, separating the quality of the decision from the quality of the outcome, in a setting where people are not defending themselves. Blame-oriented review reliably produces defensive practice and hidden errors; blame-free review produces improvement.

A fifth failure is worth naming because it happens after the incident rather than during it: revising the story. Under the pressure of guilt or of scrutiny, people reconstruct what they knew at the time to match what they learned later, and the reconstruction is usually harsher than the truth. Writing down what you actually knew, and when, protects you from your own retrospective editing as much as it serves any inquiry.

Finally, look after the people who did the sorting, including yourself. Expect delayed reactions over days and weeks: intrusive recall, sleep disturbance, guilt centred on a specific face or decision, and irritability. Most of this settles with time, rest, ordinary routine and talking to people who were there. Some of it does not, and persistent symptoms beyond a month or so warrant proper help rather than endurance. Deciding who gets help is the discipline; being the one who then needs it is not a failure of it.

guides.safetyNote: Triage systems are for situations where help is genuinely insufficient. In any ordinary emergency, call the emergency services first and treat the sickest casualty; do not withhold care on the basis of a category. Never enter an unsafe scene — fire, unstable structures, traffic, water, or confined spaces with unknown atmospheres — as a rescuer who becomes a casualty removes help from everyone. A hypothermic or cold-water casualty may appear dead and still recover, so do not declare death on appearance alone. The procedures here are a framework for thinking, not a substitute for hands-on first aid training.
